summary: Nvidia's primary competitive threat is Google's TPU, not AMD, Broadcom, Marvell, or Intel.
summary_extended: Baker argues that Nvidia's primary competitive threat is not AMD, Broadcom, Marvell, or Intel, but rather Google's TPU, framing the AI chip landscape as a binary fight between Nvidia and Google. His reasoning is that Nvidia has evolved beyond being a semiconductor company into a full-stack systems and data-center-level company, with CUDA software, NVLink, InfiniBand, and rack-level solutions creating deep switching costs that commodity chip alternatives cannot match. Google is uniquely dangerous because it is the only competitor that simultaneously owns a leading AI lab (DeepMind/Gemini) and its own silicon (TPU), giving it both the demand signal and the engineering feedback loop to iterate effectively. Baker is specifically bearish on hyperscaler ASIC programs enabled by Broadcom and Marvell, predicting most will fail within three years, particularly if Google begins selling TPUs externally and commoditizes custom silicon. The investment implication is to remain long Nvidia as the dominant infrastructure layer while being skeptical of the ASIC thesis that underpins bullish cases for Broadcom and Marvell.
detail: Baker argues Nvidia is no longer just a semiconductor company but a systems/data-center-level company (CUDA software, rack-level solutions, NVLink/InfiniBand/Ethernet fabric). The real battle is Nvidia vs. Google TPU. Google is a uniquely dangerous competitor because it owns both the chip (TPU) and a leading AI lab (DeepMind/Gemini). Broadcom is enabling hyperscaler ASICs as an alternative fabric, but Baker believes most ASIC programs will fail within three years, especially if Google begins selling TPUs externally.
